Markey, Deaton met in their only Senate debate. Here are 3 takeaways.

Deaton, two years removed from his first US Senate run against Elizabeth Warren, criticized Markey’s decades-long record in Washington and questioned whether the 80-year-old senator should — and at times overtly whether he could — serve another six years in office.Here are three takeaways from the debate hosted by WBZ-TV.US Senator Ed Markey during Tuesday's debate in Boston.WBZ-TVParty timePresident Trump’s term ends in nearly two years, but Markey repeatedly wielded him as a cudgel against Deaton, a Republican, but one who says he’s never voted for his party’s standard-bearer and called the GOP — and the Democratic Party, for good measure — “corrupt.”In the first five minutes of Tuesday’s debate, Markey framed Deaton as someone who “is going to Washington to be a blank check for Donald Trump.” “He’ll continue the majority for the Republicans,” Markey said. Deaton, a 59-year-old attorney, former Marine, and cryptocurrency booster, pushed back. “You know I never voted for President Trump,” he said, before adding: “I’m the one that is debating you, not Donald Trump.”The exchange underscored an issue that cropped up throughout the hour-long debate: which party controls the Senate, where Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority, and what it could mean for the country. To Deaton, that’s a moot question; his own party, he says, is destined to lose its grip on the chamber come November.“We all know that the Democrats are going to win the House, and the Democrats are going to win the Senate,” Deaton said. “You have a chance to send a nonpartisan person like me [to Washington] who will really put America first and decide, ‘Is it good for Massachusetts and America?’ And if it is, I’ll support it.”Markey argued that, regardless of Deaton’s promises of independence, he still has a ‘R’ next to his name. Deaton also gave the state GOP nearly $350,000 just weeks after the party’s leadership voted to endorse him last year.“He’s trying to pretend that he’s an independent and that he’s a Republican at the same time. That’s an oxymoron,” said Markey, an unabashed liberal who’s touted Medicare for All, among other progressive policies. “It’s like trying to be a carnivorous vegetarian.” Age-old issueMarkey, who would be 86 at the end of his next term should he win reelection, faced repeated criticisms from Moulton and his supporters that he should have passed the torch to the next generation instead of seeking another six-year term. That argument didn’t quite play with Democratic primary voters. But Deaton, who has pitched term limits for federal lawmakers as part of his campaign platform, pointed out that Markey “has been in office since Gerald Ford was president” and that he has run out of time to get his priorities across the finish line.“Senator Markey will be ignored. He’ll be relegated to the corner of the Senate with his little slogans,” Deaton said. “Even with his party in control, he’s never going to be heard from again until, unfortunately, he retires or passes away.”Later in the debate, Deaton said he doubted that Markey could gain traction on many of his policies in the next six years, “if you make it that long.”Markey dismissed Deaton’s criticisms “as red herrings.”“We’re going to need an aquarium right here in WBZ before the end of the night,” he quipped.Markey, for his part, has beaten back two primary challenges from younger Democrats — Moulton and, in 2020, former US representative Joe Kennedy III — who argued the junior senator is out of touch with the electorate.On Tuesday, Markey, who was first elected in 1976, highlighted more recent policy, including his push for the Green New Deal. Parts of the sweeping climate proposal, including clean energy and tax incentives, ended up in the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act.Markey said the next stage is a push for Medicare for All, which he said requires “momentum” and “movement that comes from leadership” in a Democrat-controlled Senate.Republican Senate nominee John Deaton during Tuesday's debate in Boston.WBZ-TVBlame gameThe two quibbled over who is to blame for the state’s high utility costs, single-payer health care, and the country’s history of going to war. Markey painted Deaton as someone who, if he were elected to the Senate, would oppose expanding wind and solar energy and make it “impossible for us to break our dependence upon oil and gas.”Deaton focused on Markey’s record in Congress, including his time serving on House panels aimed at energy and the environment. “Look what our energy prices are in Massachusetts,” Deaton said. “Experience is great, but if you’re cursed with bad judgment, the way Senator Markey has, it doesn’t work.”When asked about health care, Deaton agreed with Markey’s stance that Congress should pass Medicare for All, which would eliminate private insurance in place of a single-payer system. But, he said, Markey has failed to build a coalition around it. “Senator Markey, you can’t even get half of your Democratic Party to support it,” Deaton said. “You promised it six years ago.” The two also clashed over a question on when it is appropriate for the US military to go to war. Congress holds the power to declare war, which it has done 11 times. Markey slammed the Trump administration’s war in Iran.Deaton then used the opportunity to take a shot at Markey for voting to authorize the Iraq War in 2002, a vote Markey has said was a “mistake.” Samantha J. Markey and Deaton clash on debate stage as Election Day nears


									
					
Incumbent Democratic Sen. Ed Markey and Republican challenger John Deaton faced off in the final debate before Massachusetts voters head to the polls.

At the debate hosted by WBZ-TV, the two rivals went back and forth on a number of issues, including on health care and affordability.


"We do have a medical system in crisis," Markey said. "We have to have a system that finally, once and for all, reaches everyone in our nation."

"If you give me one thing to work on when I go to Washington, it will be health care," Deaton said.

Still, the Republican was critical of Markey's health care priorities.

"Medicare for all -- two thirds of the Senate Democrats don't support it," Deaton said. "I've got a real plan that breaks up the three vertically-integrated insurance companies."

								Democratic Sen. Ed Markey fended off a primary challenge from Rep. Seth Moulton and will face Republican John Deaton in November.
							
The candidates also sparred on energy costs.

Deaton said high utility bills in Massachusetts are "because of these alternative energy mandates."

Markey said that if Deaton is elected, he'll "make it impossible for us to break our dependence upon oil and gas."

Markey and Deaton agreed on a need to establish more guardrails for artificial intelligence.

"Unless we interject some accountability, Donald Trump is just going to have a moral agreement handshake with them," Markey said. "We need a Democratic Senate so we start to have the hearings on this issue."

"We need safeguards," Deaton said. "I'm scared about our seniors, I really am, because our seniors can actually be taken advantage of."

After the debate, both candidates continued to make their pitches to voters.

"If experience could fix Massachusetts, it wouldn't be so broken right now," Deaton said. "I'm here offering an alternative to the status quo."

"We need a Democratic Senate in order to finally provide a check upon Donald Trump," Markey said.

The general election will be held Nov. 3, with early voting beginning on Oct. 17 and running through Oct. 30.

Ed Markey and Republican challenger John Deaton. “As a tax-exempt non-profit, they are barred by federal law from intervening in elections — yet they deliberately blacked out our federal candidacy while promoting our opponents,” Ayyadurai alleged on social media. Advertisement:The Belmont Voice board of directors responded with a public statement Thursday, saying Ayyadurai’s complaint is “a baseless, frivolous lawsuit that we expect will be resolved quickly.”But the legal battle is also an “unpleasant” and “costly distraction” for a nonprofit with a small staff and volunteer board, the statement continued. What Ayyadurai’s lawsuit claimsAccording to his lawsuit, Ayyadurai contacted Belmont Voice leadership in late August to inquire about election coverage and was assured the newspaper’s reporting would “expand to include other candidates” following the September primary. But after the Voice published a Sept. 25 profile of Deaton, Ayyadurai followed up with repeated demands that he be interviewed as well. Advertisement:The newspaper’s board chair told Ayyadurai the editorial team was “planning further coverage of this race and does plan to include your campaign in that coverage” — a response Ayyadurai said he viewed as “constructive candidate exclusion.” In an email to the chair days later, he alleged that the Voice was racist and “must be punished” for purportedly violating his civil rights and covering his campaign unfairly, according to the lawsuit. While the Voice ultimately emailed Ayyadurai interview questions on Oct. 14, he claims the newspaper demonstrated “a consistent pattern of discriminatory disrespect, racial gatekeeping, and bad-faith minimization toward a Brown-skinned Indian immigrant candidate” by referring to him as “Mr. Ayyadurai” rather than “doctor.” (Ayyadurai, the self-described “inventor of email,” holds a Ph.D. from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.)Ayyadurai also took issue with one interview question that mischaracterized his campaign as a race for “state senate,” rather than the U.S. Senate. Massachusetts delegation asks DHS for inspection at ICE field office

“Congress and the public deserve immediate transparency about ICE’s practices, and the secretive use of this Massachusetts building as an unmonitored detention site,” the lawmakers wrote in a nine-page letter sent Thursday to the department’s Office of Inspector General.Echoing the concerns of a federal judge last month, the delegation, led by US Senator Elizabeth Warren, highlighted claims of inhumane conditions, overcrowding, due process denials, and a lack of medical care, among other deficiencies at the field office, located in a suburban business park northwest of Boston.“These reports raise serious concerns that ICE is failing to follow even its own standards for detention and short-term holding facilities,” the delegation wrote in the letter. A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security told the Globe in a statement that the Burlington field office complies with state and local law. Detainees are “quickly processed” at Burlington and then transferred to a detention facility, according to the spokesperson. “ICE is regularly audited and inspected by internal and external agencies and is committed to transparency,” the spokesperson said. “Claims of inadequate conditions at the Burlington facility are FALSE.”The facility has an “abundance of supplies,” including food, water, personal hygiene products, and bedding, DHS said. “All detainees are provided with proper meals, medical treatment, and have opportunities to communicate with lawyers and their family members,” the spokesperson said.The lawmakers’ letter, however, says attorneys representing detainees told Warren’s office of an instance where 75 women were held in a single room in Burlington, the letter reads. There was only one exposed toilet, and many of the women had to stand overnight because there was not enough space. Several of the women fainted, according to the delegation.“These atrocious conditions appear to persist for detainees held for long periods of time,” the letter reads.The letter cites the Globe’s reporting on the facility, including the case of a woman who was 24 weeks pregnant when she was detained by ICE earlier this year and rushed to the hospital in acute abdominal pain. The delegation also spotlighted the Globe’s reporting on the case of 29-year-old Brazilian woman living in Malden, who had recently experienced a miscarriage, was undergoing a mental health crisis, and suffering from an infection, when she was taken into ICE custody. When the woman, Iara do Carmo Santana, arrived at Burlington, she later told the Globe, she received no medical evaluation — despite telling officials about her health challenges — and was not given adequate access to her antibiotics for the infection. The letter to DHS comes just weeks before the 2026 midterm elections, in which Democrats hope they can flip the House and possibly the Senate as public opinion on Trump has turned sharply negative.Though Democratic elected officials in Massachusetts have repeatedly decried the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement tactics, they’ve had little power as the minority party at the federal level to enact any change. The administration has met the legislators’ criticisms with silence, or in some cases, with explicit pushback signaling that the administration’s mass deportation agenda was going to move forward no matter what.Flipping the House and/or Senate wouldn’t necessarily give Democrats an instant ability to change that, but it would give them slightly more leverage. They would have greater investigatory powers in congressional committees, and greater say over annual government funding bills that could come with conditions for federal agencies or pull back some of the billions that Republicans passed to fund immigration enforcement. Still, Trump would likely have to agree to any bill for it to become law. In the meantime, however, it remains to be seen whether the federal government will move to address any of the allegations of poor conditions at the Burlington ICE field office.The lawmakers addressed their letter to Joseph V. Cuffari, the Department of Homeland Security’s inspector general, whose office provides oversight through audits, evaluations, inspections, and other checks on DHS-related activities. The office also has the authority to conduct unannounced oversight visits of ICE facilities. Senator Warren and US Representative Lori Trahan conducted their own unannounced visit to the Burlington facility on Sept. 8, the delegation wrote in their letter. The lawmakers saw more than two dozen people being held for processing — but were not allowed to talk to them directly, and they were not told that some of the detainees had been there for more than 12 hours.But days later, they learned through the Globe’s reporting that do Carmo Santana, the Malden immigrant who suffered a miscarriage, had been held there for approximately four days, and was ordered released on the day they visited. Women are often held for long periods at Burlington in part because there are no ICE holding facilities for women in Massachusetts. About a month earlier, a different woman had been held there for approximately 20 days, they noted in the letter, citing a story from the New Bedford Light. The lawmakers cited other concerns about the medical care detainees receive in Burlington. They said one woman from Ecuador who suffered from severe epilepsy was not given the medication she needed during her detention in Burlington and suffered a seizure at the facility in an overcrowded cell. “ICE has repeatedly evaded accountability about its treatment of detainees at the Burlington facility,” the delegation said. Since the Trump administration began increasing its immigration enforcement activities across the region last year, immigrants and their attorneys have taken their cases to federal court — submitting habeas corpus cases which allege that federal immigration agents have unlawfully detained petitioners.The petitions have, at times, overwhelmed the courts in New England and across the country — and federal judges in Massachusetts have in several cases admonished ICE for holding immigrants in inadequate conditions at the Burlington field office. The letter from the Massachusetts delegation points to comments made by Judge Leo T. Sorokin in a case from July, in which a woman was held at the Burlington facility for almost a week. He ordered her released, writing clearly in his order: “The Burlington Field Office is not an appropriate facility for the overnight custody of individuals.”Sorokin also oversaw the habeas case of do Carmo Santana, and in a September hearing after said that while federal immigration authorities were allowed to take people into custody — but they had a constitutional responsibility to take care of them.“You owe them medical care,” Sorokin told the US attorney’s office in court. “I view that as a serious issue.”The delegation also said that ICE denied Massachusetts Representative Katherine Clark entrance to the facility in February, and that the agency has “consistency failed” to provide answers from their offices about the treatment of detainees.In addition to conducting an inspection of the Burlington field office, the delegation requested that the Office of Inspector General answer more than two dozen questions concerning the conditions at the facility. John Deaton's biggest challenge isn't Ed Markey. It's President Trump | WBUR News

Support WBUR04:12John Deaton, Republican candidate for U.S. Senate, in front of his campaign bus in Stoneham. (Anthony Brooks/WBUR)John Deaton made his pitch to a handful of residents inside a Malden retirement home: He's a fan of good ideas, period. It doesn't matter if those ideas are "progressive or conservative, Democrat or Republican," he said."If it's good for Massachusetts and America, I'll support it. If it isn't, I won't," Deaton, the Republican candidate for Senate, said to a smattering of applause.John Deaton, Republican candidate for U.S. Senate, talks with a resident at Forestdale Park in Malden. (Anthony Brooks/WBUR)Deaton knows he faces an uphill fight in a state that hasn't sent a Republican to the U.S. Senate since Scott Brown won in 2010. With just a month to go until the election, polls suggest Deaton is running well behind Sen. Ed Markey, the Democratic incumbent he's hoping to unseat. But his lowkey, moderate political pitch impressed a number of the residents in Malden."It was very refreshing to hear someone not bash other politicians," said Mary Jane Peloso, an independent, who liked that Deaton expressed a willingness to break ranks with his own party."I didn't know anything about him but I'm really going to consider voting for him," Peloso said.Deaton, a Marine veteran and attorney, grew up poor outside of Detroit. He's faced significant obstacles in his life, including battles with cancer and addiction. But running for the U.S. Senate as a Republican in Massachusetts — where President Trump might be less popular than King George at the Boston Tea Party — may be his biggest challenge yet."The challenge for me is to get people to look beyond the label, but it is a big hurdle," Deaton told WBUR.It was a hurdle Deaton couldn't clear two years ago when he ran against Sen. Elizabeth Warren. But he said, now more than ever, Massachusetts needs someone who can stand up to both parties, a sentiment he so memorably expressed earlier this fall:"F the Republican Party. F the Democrat Party. They all suck," he said during his debate with Congressman Seth Moulton before the primary.Deaton considered running as an independent but concluded the route wasn't politically viable. So he's running as a non-MAGA, pro-abortion-rights Republican, who says he would bring "balance and independence" to the the Senate."I really, truly would work with a Democrat. I would truly work with Trump," he said.On the day he visited the retirement home in Malden, Deaton also found support outside a Stop & Shop in Stoneham, where Republican candidate for state representative Stephen Ternullo was holding a sign for his own campaign. Ternullo said he's backing Deaton because "Markey has been in Washington too long.""I grew up in Medford and Ed Markey's been in there since I was 5 years old," Ternullo said. "His way of thinking is gone and we need some fresh ideas. And John Deaton is a fresh idea."Deaton parts company with Trump on a number of key issues, including the war with Iran and tariffs. On immigration, Deaton said ICE needs to be reformed, not abolished as Markey wants. And he called Markey's push for Medicare for All misguided because most Democrats in the Senate don't support it. Instead, Deaton favors breaking up the big insurance companies."We can achieve and fix healthcare, but not if you're insisting on a plan that you can't even get your party to agree with," Deaton said.Deaton and Markey will face off in their only scheduled debate Tuesday night, when Markey will no doubt try to link Deaton to Trump, as he did after he won the Democratic primary last month."Massachusetts does not want to have a MAGA Republican representing them in the Senate," Markey told NBC Boston.Sen. Ed Markey (D-MA) is seen at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C. on July 23. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)Deaton pushed back and said he's not part of MAGA, has never voted for Trump, and were he to win, he would not do Trump's bidding."I got spit at by Trump Republicans," Deaton said, recalling his first Senate run two years ago. "I got called RINO, a piece of you-know-what and I never caved."After all that, Deaton said he wouldn't go to Washington and "give in to a guy who's not goinng be president four out of the six years, who's in a much weaker position."Deaton accused Markey of deliberately mischaracterizing him."It angers me," he said, urging Markey to debate "my ideas  instead of just labeling me something that I'm not."But Markey's campaign manager, Cam Charbonnier, told WBUR that "a vote for Deaton is a vote to continue the Republican majority in the Senate and the Trump agenda."So, Deaton presses on. He said he's eager to find out if he can attract enough Republicans and moderate independents to pull off what would be a seismic upset on Nov. 3. But he conceded that it's a longshot, and that the label "Republican" in Massachusetts — especially with Trump in the White House — could make that "just an impossible task."It's all part of John Deaton's challenge as he runs for the Senate, while running away from Trump.This segment aired on October 13, 2026.2026 Election

Suffolk/Globe poll: 42% say Mass. has become worse place to live

About 59 percent of the 500 likely general election voters surveyed said they would back Healey for a second term, while 36 percent planned to vote for Minogue, the former Abiomed executive who has cast the state as too expensive and insufficiently governed. Less than 4 percent of voters remained undecided — including some who were surveyed after two debates between the candidates — suggesting Minogue has little opportunity to woo disaffected voters.One might think, given voter unhappiness, that Minogue could have more potential converts. While more than half of respondents said they believed Massachusetts was headed in the right direction, only 15 percent said the state has become a better place to live over the last four years.By comparison, about 42 percent — a plurality — said they believed the state had gotten worse to some degree. Another 40 percent said they believed it has remained the same. Still, the survey’s results emphasized that Massachusetts voters’ enduring distaste for President Trump supersedes more parochial concerns. Nearly three in four voters surveyed said they had an unfavorable view of Trump, whose wide-scale immigrant deportation campaign and sweeping tariff policies have regularly played into Healey’s campaign strategy of insisting the president is “on the ballot.”Healey has sought to tie Minogue to Trump, highlighting her rival’s donation of hundreds of thousands of dollars to Trump’s second campaign. More than 60 percent of voters said a Republican candidate with a history of voting for or supporting Trump would either make it less likely to support or entirely disqualify a candidate in their view, the poll found.David Paleologos, director of the Suffolk University Political Research Center, said much of Minogue’s campaign message was “validated in this poll.” Specifically, many voters seemed to agree with his position on taxes (55 percent said they’re too high) and the state economy (58 percent described it as fair or poor).But Minogue, he said, didn’t correctly calculate “how toxic his proximity to President Trump would be.”“That was an expensive mistake because Trump’s favorability is so low that anyone remotely associated with or supportive of him . . . is going to be impacted,” Paleologos said. “Minogue’s got the right messages, but he’s the wrong messenger at the wrong time.”Voters appear to hold the federal government as responsible for Massachusetts’ fiscal outlook as the state’s chief executive. About 33 percent of voters said they felt Trump was most responsible for Massachusetts’ economy, compared with 34 percent  who felt that responsibility lay with Healey.Brian Julin, a 55-year-old Democrat from South Hadley, is one of the 42 percent of voters who believe the quality of life in Massachusetts has declined over the last four years. But he attributes much of that to changes launched by the Trump administration. Healey, he said, has “been doing a decent job, given the conditions that she has to work under.”“Higher [education] is an export industry the size of soybeans, and we’re losing a lot of our actual export capability because foreign students are not coming here as much,” Julin, who works at a local university, said of why he believes Massachusetts has gotten “a little worse.” He added: “I’m not going to say it’s entirely the federal government’s fault, but it’s mostly the feds’ fault.”Elizabeth Michaud, a professional astrologer from Salisbury, said that while the “cost of everything is unbelievable” in Massachusetts, she believes the Trump administration has worsened affordability issues. $130M grant will upgrade Springfield train system, support West-East Rail


									
					
A $130 million federal grant will support rail upgrades in Springfield, Massachusetts, work that will help bring the West-East Rail plan to life, the governor's office announced on Friday.

MassDOT secured the funding through the Federal Railroad Administration's (FRA) Fiscal Years 2025-2026 Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements (CRISI) grant program, the Healey administration announced on Friday. It will go toward the Springfield Hub Modernization Project, which includes investment in the existing Connecticut River Line and moves forward plans for the proposed West-East Rail.


The current phase focuses on Springfield's Union Station as a hub and would build out service on the existing Amtrak Vermonter, Hartford Line and Valley Flyer lines. The larger West-East Rail proposal is a vision to connect Albany, Springfield, Boston and other cities via passenger train service.

“This is a major win for Western Massachusetts and a big step forward for West-East Rail,” said Gov. Maura Healey in a media statement. “This $130 million investment in Springfield will help us improve transportation, reduce congestion and connect more communities to jobs, housing and economic opportunity. 

This phase of the project would focus on upgrading tracks, signals and other infrastructure, and help reduce conflict points between freight and passenger trains. This will help create the capacity needed for future passenger rail service through the area. 

“Building West-East rail is a once-in a-lifetime investment to connect Massachusetts’ communities and our regional economies like never before. It will mean lower costs, less congestion, and access to opportunity for families across the state,” Sen. Ed Markey said in a media release.

Consistent, reliable rail service has long been missing from western Massachusetts. Currently there is just one Amtrak train per day between Albany and Boston, a trip that takes more than five hours.

Democratic senators set up vote on blocking Saudi nuclear deal

Sens. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) and Ed Markey (D-Mass.) introduced a measure Thursday that would block President Trump's deal to allow Saudi Arabia to build a civilian nuclear program. The Democrats' measure is a joint resolution of disapproval, a legislative tool that requires a vote after Nov. 29.The senators expressed concern that the deal gives Saudi Arabia access to U.S. technology for civilian nuclear energy but does not contain sufficient guardrails against Riyadh using that tech to create nuclear weapons. "It is essential that nations pursuing civilian energy programs agree to the 'gold standard' of restrictions on fuel reprocessing and enrichment and rigorous inspections to ensure that a nuclear energy program doesn't become a covert nuclear weapons program," Merkley said in a press release.Trump inked the deal with the Saudi government in late July to allow U.S. companies to develop Saudi Arabia's nuclear energy infrastructure over 30 years. It does not need approval from Congress but will not go into effect until a 90-day window has closed, giving lawmakers time to debate if they want to block the deal. Democrats in the House have introduced an identical measure. But both resolutions face tall odds, as they need a signature from Trump to reverse the deal, which is improbable.Trump said at the time that the deal would hinge on Saudi Arabia joining the Abraham Accords, a regional treaty centered on normalization of relations with Israel that Trump brokered in 2020. That is not part of the deal signed by Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman, but Wright told reporters at the time that negotiations over the accords would "be worked in parallel" with the progress of the nuclear deal. While Republican senators generally support the deal, some indicated at the time they wanted more information about the constraints the agreement would put on nuclear weapons development. "So I think the positive is they've become a member of the Abraham Accords, which I think is a big deal in trying to create peace in the Middle East, so I think that's a real positive," Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) told reporters in July. "I don't know enough detail about the limitations of their usage. I want to understand that better."Sen. Edward John Markey (born July 11, 1946) is an American politician serving as the junior United States senator from the state of Massachusetts, a seat he has held since 2013. A member of the Democratic Party, he served 20 terms (18 full, two partial) as the U.S. representative for Massachusetts's 7th congressional district from 1976 to 2013. Before that, he was a member of the Massachusetts House of Representatives from 1973 to 1976. He has been the dean of Massachusetts's congressional delegation since 2009.
In 2013, after John Kerry was appointed United States Secretary of State, Markey was elected to serve out the remainder of Kerry's Senate term in a 2013 special election. Markey defeated Stephen Lynch in the Democratic primary and Republican Gabriel E. Gomez in the general election. He was elected to a full term in the Senate in 2014. Markey fended off a primary challenge from Joseph Kennedy III and was reelected in 2020 by a wide margin.
Markey is a progressive who has focused on climate change and energy policy and chaired the House Select Committee on Energy Independence and Global Warming from 2007 to 2011. He is the Senate author of the Green New Deal[1] and is a member of the Senate Fight Club.[2] Markey is running for reelection against John Deaton in 2026.
Early life and education[edit]
Markey in the Boston College yearbook, 1968
Markey was born on July 11, 1946, in Malden, Massachusetts, the son of Christina M. (née Courtney) and John E. Markey, a milkman. Markey's mother was the valedictorian of her high school class but was unable to attend college because her mother died and she was needed to care for the family.[3][4][5] The family was Irish Catholic, and Markey was educated at Immaculate Conception School and Malden Catholic High School.[6]
Starting in the summer of 1965, Markey was the driver and salesperson for an ice cream truck in Lexington, Massachusetts. He was known as "Eddie the Ice Cream Man" to neighborhood children and used the proceeds from the HP Hood route to pay tuition at Boston College. In the late 1960s Markey was cited by the Lexington Police for the ringing of his bell to announce the ice cream truck's presence. Soon after the citation, the selectmen of Lexington changed the ordinance and he was allowed to ring his bell.[7]
Markey graduated from Boston College in 1968 with a Bachelor of Arts and from Boston College Law School in 1972 with a Juris Doctor.[8]
Edward Markey, 1975
After graduating, Markey worked as a lawyer in private practice. He served in the United States Army Reserve from 1968 to 1973, attaining the rank of Specialist 4.[9] He joined while a junior in college, and has said that he enlisted before knowing whether he would receive a Vietnam War draft notice.[9][a] Markey also said that even though he opposed the war, he would have answered the induction notice and gone to Vietnam if he had been drafted, despite having secured a position in the Reserve.[9] His South Boston reserve unit included Thomas P. O'Neill III, Steve Grossman, and Markey's brothers Richard and John.[9][11]
Markey was elected to the Massachusetts House of Representatives, where he represented the 16th Middlesex district (Malden and Melrose) and 26th Middlesex district from 1973 to 1976.[12][13]
U.S. House of Representatives[edit]
Markey during the 101st United States Congress (1989)
On May 21, 1976, incumbent Congressman Torbert Macdonald died in office.[14] Markey, who had just been elected to a third term in the state house, entered a twelve-candidate Democratic primary[15] for what was then the 7th district. In the primary—the real contest in this heavily Democratic district—Markey won the nomination with a plurality of 22% of the vote.[16] In the November 1976 election he defeated Republican Richard Daly 77%–18%.[17] That election doubled as both a special election for the balance of Macdonald's 11th term and a regular election for a full two-year term, and so Markey took office later that night. This gave him greater seniority than other Representatives first elected in 1976.
Markey was challenged in a Democratic primary three times, first in 1980, when he won 85%;[18] then in 1984, when he won 54%;[19] and finally in 2002, when he won 85% of the vote.[20]
Markey was reelected 19 more times from this district, which included most of the northern suburbs of Boston. His lowest vote total was 62% in 1992, in a three-way election. Markey faced no Republican opposition in eight of his bids for reelection, in 1978, 1980, 1986, 1988, 1990, 2000, 2002, and 2006.[21][22] His district was renumbered the 5th after the 2010 census, in which Massachusetts lost a district.
Markey as ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee
Markey was a member of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, and the National Journal gave him a "Composite Liberal" score of 89.2.[23]
Environment and energy[edit]
In December 2007, Markey became the first US politician to use Second Life, through which he addressed the delegates of the UNFCCC in Bali as part of OneClimate's Virtual Bali event. It was estimated that the carbon dioxide he saved by not flying to Bali was around 5.5 tons.[24] Pressure from Markey prompted BP to provide a live underwater video feed showing oil leaking out of a pipe in the Deepwater Horizon oil spill in 2010.[25] Markey has been a longtime critic of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) and has been critical of the NRC's decision-making on the proposed Westinghouse AP1000 reactor design and the NRC response to the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster.[26][27]
In reply to Alaska's Governor Sarah Palin's position on how the American Clean Energy and Security Act (also known as Waxman-Markey, named after Markey and Henry Waxman) could have a negative impact for Alaskans,[28] Markey wrote an article criticizing Palin's inaction on global warming and her environmental positions.[29]
Markey sarcastically suggested in August 2010 that global warming deniers form their own country on an iceberg: "An iceberg four times the size of Manhattan has broken off Greenland, creating plenty of room for global warming deniers to start their own country." Markey also said that, at the time, 2010 was the hottest recorded year and that "scientists agree Arctic ice is a canary in a coal mine that provides clear warnings on climate".[30][31] Markey has derided Republicans' stance on global warming, stating during a hearing: "I won't physically rise, because I'm worried that Republicans will overturn the law of gravity, sending us floating about the room."[32]
In January 2011, House Republicans eliminated the Select Committee for Energy Independence and Global Warming, which Nancy Pelosi created in 2006 and Markey chaired.[33]
Objection to certifying the 2004 U.S. presidential election results[edit]
Markey was one of the 31 House Democrats who voted not to count Ohio's 20 electoral votes in the 2004 U.S. presidential election.[34] In 2004, President George W. Bush (the Republican nominee) had defeated Senator John Kerry (the Democratic nominee) in Ohio by 118,457 votes.[35] Without Ohio's electoral votes, the 2004 presidential election would have been decided by the U.S. House of Representatives, with each state having one vote, as dictated by the Twelfth Amendment to the United States Constitution.
Domestic initiatives[edit]
Markey introduced legislation to change the duration of Daylight Saving Time[36] and to increasing privacy controls over children online.[37]
Markey drew some controversy through his proposal to introduce legislation[38] that deals with amusement parks' roller coasters, believing that newer, faster rides that exert greater G-pressures on the human body are dangerous mentally and physically, despite a lack of concrete evidence to support these claims,[39] and contrary to studies that affirmed the safety of roller coasters in general.[40]
